blocks.text: 1. KNN

blocks.alt: A query goes through K nearest neighbors to produce top-K results

blocks.text: KNN, the classic algorithm for finding the K nearest neighbors to a query, generalizes single nearest neighbor search into something far more useful.
It returns the K closest stored vectors to a query, not just the single closest one.
2. From One Neighbor To K
Brute force search, as covered previously, found only the single closest vector; most real queries want several relevant results.
KNN generalizes that idea to return K neighbors instead of just one.
3. Choosing K

blocks.alt: A small K is compared against a large K

blocks.text: A small K returns only the most confident matches; a larger K returns a broader, more diverse set.
That choice directly shapes how much context a downstream system receives.

blocks.text: 4. KNN Is An Algorithm Not An Index

blocks.alt: KNN is compared against an index structure

blocks.text: KNN describes what to compute, not how to compute it efficiently, unlike an index as covered in Indexing.
A naive KNN implementation is just brute force search with K results kept instead of one.
5. Sorting Cost At Scale

blocks.alt: All distances are sorted, then the top K are taken

blocks.text: Finding the top K still requires touching every vector at least once, the same linear scaling problem brute force search runs into.
Sorting or partially sorting those distances adds further cost on top of that comparison.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: Naive KNN computes a distance to every vector and then sorts the entire result list, even though only the smallest K values actually matter, wasting effort on ranking distances that get discarded.

blocks.text: 6. Using A Heap For Efficiency

blocks.alt: All distances go through a heap of size K to produce top K

blocks.text: Maintaining a small heap of the current best K candidates avoids a full sort of every distance.
It is a practical optimization that still leaves the core linear scan intact.
7. KNN As The Foundation For ANN

blocks.alt: Exact KNN leads to the approximate version, ANN

blocks.text: Every ANN algorithm still aims to approximate this same K nearest neighbors goal, a preview already raised in Indexing.
KNN defines the target; ANN algorithms find faster ways to approach it.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: Every algorithm covered across the rest of this module aims to return results as close as possible to what exact KNN would return, just faster, making KNN the conceptual target every ANN method is measured against.

blocks.text: 8. K Sensitivity In Retrieval
Too few neighbors can miss relevant context; too many can dilute it, the same retrieval precision concern raised in Why Chunking.
Tuning K is a real, practical decision every retrieval pipeline has to make.

blocks.text: 9. Recognizing How To Choose K For A Retrieval Pipeline

blocks.alt: Needing more context chunks points toward increasing K

blocks.text: Precise, narrow queries suit a smaller K.
Broad, exploratory queries benefit from a larger K to capture more context.

blocks.text: 11. Common Mistakes

items: Sorting the entire distance list when only the top K values are actually needed.
Choosing a fixed K without considering how narrow or broad a given query actually is.
Confusing KNN, an algorithm, with an index, a structure that makes it run efficiently.
Assuming a single K value works equally well for every kind of retrieval query.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

items: KNN returns the K closest stored vectors to a query, generalizing single nearest neighbor search.
A small K returns confident matches; a larger K returns a broader, more diverse set.
KNN describes what to compute, not how to compute it efficiently, unlike an index.
Naive KNN still requires touching every vector, plus the added cost of sorting distances.
Maintaining a small heap of the current best K candidates avoids a full sort of every distance.
Every ANN algorithm still aims to approximate the same K nearest neighbors goal KNN defines.
Too few neighbors can miss relevant context; too many can dilute it with less relevant matches.
Tuning K is a real, practical decision every retrieval pipeline has to make.
